The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • According to recent reports, boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

According to recent reports, boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

It has been revealed that key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

Sources indicate that in their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

According to recent reports, two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s key to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” remarked Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another substantial expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Sources indicate that adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

In a recent development, baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

Recent findings suggest that but their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

In a recent development, millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

Recent findings suggest that that dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze reveals up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Recent findings suggest that consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

According to recent reports, this analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Recent findings suggest that home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

In a recent development, income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

In a recent development, share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

According to recent reports, how to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

Nvidia, IBM and Fermilab unveiled upcoming tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

It has been revealed that nvidia released a new decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the company, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia stated that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.".

Nvidia and IBM also declared aims for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," remarked Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

Sources indicate that IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform.".

Recent findings suggest that in 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a upcoming output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

How an Artsy Pennsylvania River Town Became an Architectural Powerhouse Where Old Meets New

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, New Hope, PA, looks like little more than a picturesque, upscale river town with a vibrant arts scene.
  • Located halfway between New York City and Philadelphia, New Hope spans roughly 1.42 square miles and is home to fewer than 3,000 year-round residents.
  • In Latest Hope's luxury housing market, old and new blend seamlessly: 18th-century structures are brought into the 21st century with bold, modern additions and amenities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, New Hope, PA, looks like little more than a picturesque, upscale river town with a vibrant arts scene. However, a closer look reveals that the historic borough shares an architectural DNA with Europe's premier capitals.

Located halfway between New York City and Philadelphia, New Hope spans roughly 1.42 square miles and is home to fewer than 3,000 year-round residents. Yet it boasts an outsized reputation as a beloved regional tourist destination renowned for its art galleries, boutiques, riverside dining, and cultural institutions, led by the iconic Bucks County Playhouse, which has hosted major stars such as Grace Kelly, Robert Redford, and Liza Minnelli.

In Latest Hope's luxury housing market, old and new blend seamlessly: 18th-century structures are brought into the 21st century with bold, modern additions and amenities.

"A lot of the homes around here, especially some of the larger homes, all started off as an old stone farmhouse, so incorporating some of that character while building the substantial steel and glass additions is very much an architectural vibe that is done here," Nicholas Esser, managing partner at Addison Wolfe Real Estate, tells Realtor.com®.

The market's remarkably varied housing stock also includes stately Colonial and Victorian homes, sprawling legacy estates, and cutting-edge fresh construction that would not look out of place in the heart of Silicon Valley.

It has been revealed that architect Ralph Fey, with Ralph C. Fey Architects in Doylestown, PA, explains that New Hope's signature look is rooted in regulatory necessity, because more than half of the town falls in a strictly regulated historic district, which rarely allows older buildings to be torn down to make way for new builds.

Rather than viewing zoning laws as a creative roadblock, Fey has made his professional mark by seamlessly merging history with contemporary living.

Industry observers note that "Some of the best architecture is born out of constraints," he tells Realtor.com. "The goal, the fun, the challenge is how to maintain that historic feel, meet the guidelines of the historic district, but provide the amenities that we now want to have as we live on the water.".

It has been revealed that maureen Reynolds, a Serhant luxury real estate agent in Upcoming Hope, counts herself among Fey's clients. She currently lives in an 1832-built converted horse barn with tall ceilings and hand-hewn beams.

"I have all the modern amenities because of Ralph," she tells Realtor.com.

While New Hope lacks the urban density and wealth of major metros, Fey notes, its architectural style "is more like London, where you have newer construction next to historic construction, next to really historic construction, and it is that fabric that makes London so exciting.".

Founded in the 18th century on the banks of the Delaware River, New Hope was previously called Wells Ferry and later Coryell’s Ferry.

The borough was rechristened after a fire in 1790 destroyed several mills owned by local businessman Benjamin Parry. He rebuilt them as the New Hope Mills, inspiring the town’s optimistic new name.

By the late 19th century, Fresh Hope had gained a reputation as an art colony and emerged as a major hub for American and Pennsylvania Impressionists, including William Langson Lathrop, Edward Willis Redfield, and Daniel Garber.

Recent findings suggest that "New Hope definitely has an architectural richness that's been developed over centuries," says Reynolds. "Its historic buildings' relationship to the river and surrounding landscape give it a character that cannot be created overnight. And the challenge and opportunity for the architects, for Realtors®, and for developers is to respect that history while designing homes that accommodate the way people live today.".

Fey agrees, maintaining that New Hope's success as a thriving housing market is rooted in its past and the borough's fierce commitment to protecting it.

Industry observers note that "The same little river town 5 miles down the road that did not have a historic district, where all the homes were knocked down, would not have that feel of a classic historic town, and would not have that charm, and it could potentially lose it," he indicates. "It's really notable to us as architects to preserve that feeling, and that's part of the reason why Newly introduced Hope is as prized and treasured as it is—it's for its history.".

Even with latest construction, a premium is placed on designing in harmony with the town.

Fey and Reynolds frequently work with clients to select natural building materials such as locally sourced stone, cedar wood, and slate roof tiles. They complement surrounding centuries-old structures rather than clashing with the local aesthetic.

According to recent reports, "Most of my clients are very in love with the feel of the historic Upcoming Hope and also would like to see some of the amenities of slightly more glass, slightly higher ceilings," indicates the architect. "So when we are doing additions on the traditional homes or existing historic housing stock, our goal is to contribute to the street.".

Despite its modest size, Fresh Hope commands an impressively broad appeal. Esser and Fey say buyers range from locals looking to upgrade or build their dream homes to affluent transplants from neighboring New York, Philadelphia, and New Jersey hunting for a primary residence or weekend pied-à-terre, alongside retirees drawn to Pennsylvania's favorable tax climate.

Some home shoppers, however, come from much farther afield.

Reynolds’ roster of Latest Hope clients includes buyers from the South of France, Sweden, Canada, and Japan, cementing the town’s status as a market punching well above its weight.

Recent findings suggest that in August, the Philadelphia Business Journal ranked New Hope as the nation's No. 2 hottest luxury housing market during the second quarter of 2026 among 327 markets analyzed.

"That's an extraordinary distinction for a community of this size," notes Reynolds.

Prices have surged accordingly. Reynolds recounts how townhomes originally priced between $1.4 million and $1.8 million jumped to $2 million–$3.2 million in less than three years.

The latest Realtor.com housing data demonstrates that in October, the median listing price in New Hope topped $2 million, up more than 27% from a year ago.

Meanwhile, the luxury-tier threshold—representing the top 10% of the market—was just over $5 million.

While inventory was up more than 50% year over year last month, Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones notes that supply still remains nearly 60% below pre-pandemic levels.

“Demand comes largely from cash-rich buyers in the surrounding region, including a growing share from Newly introduced Jersey alongside the New York metro, who are insulated from mortgage rates hovering around 7%,” she notes.

As always with real estate, location remains paramount.

"If I have something on the river, it usually sells within a couple days, and that can be something, too, that is not turnkey—we're talking about something that can be slightly a shell inside," says Reynolds.

Ultimately, what keeps buyers flocking to Latest Hope from near and far is the sheer architectural variety packed into the pint-sized, picture-perfect historic borough.

"The beautiful thing around here is that there's gorgeous properties everywhere, and the home styles do change between the more modern construction, with the beams and 12-foot ceilings, and old stone construction, but they mesh really well," concludes Esser.

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

In a recent development, the Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

In a recent development, investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

Sources indicate that as per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Firm, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Industry observers note that the Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) showed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

In a recent development, notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

According to recent reports, as per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

It has been revealed that since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

In its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

Breaking: 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • It has been revealed that access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

It has been revealed that access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely indicates you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

In a recent development, one had stopped going to the program’s upgrade calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same firm that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

According to recent reports, real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

Industry observers note that in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

According to recent reports, if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

Sources indicate that how to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Recent findings suggest that say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

According to recent reports, now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

In a recent development, many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

Industry observers note that how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Recent findings suggest that many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

Industry observers note that how to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Recent findings suggest that commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your strategy, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California-born sculptor Chester Beach worked out of a Upcoming York City studio between 1907 and 1952, nabbing high-profile commissions from the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, as well as the 1928 Summer Olympics.

But, like many artists, he carved out space for a pastoral retreat away from the hustle and bustle.

In 1917, after living in Rome for a brief period, he and his wife, Eleanor Beach, established a home in Brewster, NY, in Putnam County, just 55 miles north of the city. They named the Arts & Crafts-style estate OldWalls.

Now these 10.49 acres—including four buildings, comprising a compound—is looking for a latest steward.

Sources indicate that "There have only been three owners including the original family that owned it up until 2009," says listing agent Will Stuart, of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Newly introduced England Properties. "My sellers have been there for two years.".

Listing for $4,150,000, the newly introduced owner won't be the first to seek a deeper connection to nature while still being close to Manhattan.

Stuart notes that this eight-bedroom, 6.5-bath spread is exceptionally tied to its origins.

According to recent reports, "Each owner has become a steward of the property and has preserved extensive family photographs, memoirs and documents, and have really kept the story going, which is rare with these kinds of properties," he claims. "A lot of times the information gets lost along the way. The story has been preserved so well.".

According to recent reports, the estate includes a four-bedroom stone residence with plaster walls, hand-crafted stonework and stained glass. There’s also a separate guest studio with a kitchen, bath, sleeping loft and stone fireplace. And, a two-bedroom guest cottage dating back to the 1940s with cozy amenities such as a fireplace and screened-in porch.

Another way the property has been preserved is through art the original owners brought into the house.

Tiles collected from Spain, Guatemala and Italy are laid into the floor, states Stuart. He adds that "there’s actually a cluster of Roman floor tiles under the dining-room table.".

Industry observers note that the kitchen’s chandelier was born out of a turntable Beach used for sculpting. Eleanor’s bird paintings (112 in all) are incorporated into the living room’s ceiling.

“There’s three outbuildings in addition to the main residence that all offer incredible living space and charm,” notes Stuart. “Each one of them has a story and a history.”.

For example, in the detached studio, which was built before the home, are many of Beach’s tools and hardware, as well as the original doors.

A buyer drawn to that history is who Stuart is courting. But it could also be an equestrian, as the property features a five-stall barn with a spacious one-bedroom apartment. Nearby are run-outs, rolling grass turnout paddocks, a riding field with access to trails, and a riding arena in the sand.

It has been revealed that “We have a lot of equestrians that have moved into the community,” says Stuart. “A lot of the equestrian people travel to Florida in the winter so they’re here half the year, but most people are here year-round.” Two miles down the road is Old Salem Farm, a 120-acre boarding and training facility.

Above all, the buyer will likely be someone who likes to be near Manhattan but also have a countryside retreat, just like Beach once did.

Recent findings suggest that this mirrors a trend Stuart continues to see among buyers. “People looking for more space, more privacy, but want to stay within close proximity to the city,” he claims. “This is a real compound here. It’s someone who is hosting family or guests.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most important open question in mathematics.
  • Levent Alpöge declared his discovery today on his personal website.
  • “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:28 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most important open question in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge declared his discovery today on his personal website. Anthropic has not published an official announcement about the news. The manufacturer floated on the Nasdaq a day earlier in a landmark public offering that raised over $93 billion.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement. “What I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”.

In a recent development, the Riemann hypothesis was proposed in the mid-1800s by its namesake, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It focuses on a specific mathematical function, the Riemann zeta function, that was discovered more than a century earlier. A function is similar to a software program: It takes a piece of data as input and outputs another piece of data. A function’s input and output can be numbers, other functions and many other mathematical objects.

It has been revealed that the Riemann zeta function’s input and output are both complex numbers. Complex numbers share similarities with regular numbers, but also have many additional properties. When the inputs and outputs of the Riemann zeta function are visualized, they resemble a three-dimensional spiral.

The Riemann hypothesis is concerned with a specific section of that 3D spiral. In that section, the complex numbers outputted by the Riemann zeta function all equal zero. The hypothesis argues that the inputs from which those outputs are derived all include the value ½.

Sources indicate that the hypothesis is considered to be the most key open problem in mathematics for multiple reasons. The first is that although it focuses on a single, not overly complicated mathematical function, its implications extend to a far bigger topic: prime numbers. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, a seemingly random aspect of prime numbers is in fact regulated by a pattern.

Recent findings suggest that another factor behind the hypothesis’ importance is that hundreds of theorems operate on the assumption that it’s true. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, those theorems are correct as well.

Alpöge wrote that Claude proved not only the standard version of the Riemann hypothesis but also the so-called generalized variant. The latter conjecture argues that the Riemann hypothesis holds true for not only the Riemann zeta function but also certain other, similar functions. Alpöge believes that Claude will be capable of proving an even broader version of the hypothesis in the future.

The researcher detailed that Claude’s proof runs for more than 250,000 pages. He has not yet released the paper. He did, however, publish a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used to verify mathematical results. The file contains millions of lines of code.

Proofs implemented in Lean are essentially regular software programs. If a Lean program runs without crashing, the mathematical argument that it describes is correct. That makes it easier for mathematicians to verify newly published proofs.

Industry News: Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • Industry observers note that several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • The company unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Industry observers note that several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it indicates can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sources indicate that sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

It has been revealed that compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

According to recent reports, MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Sources indicate that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the problem in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He stated Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the manufacturer’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

It has been revealed that amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS declared plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

Sources indicate that the growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

According to recent reports, compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The firm did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

According to recent reports, below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

Ripple's Schwartz Reveals Why XRP Ledger Used Satoshi's Code

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.
  • 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet mentioned that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Industry observers note that some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating upcoming ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," mentioned Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a new cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz remarked it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

"It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz said.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.

#87748. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1148 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that turn closings into case studies.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

According to recent reports, most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to initiative. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

Industry observers note that we recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

In a recent development, not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

According to recent reports, this has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

Industry observers note that I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

In a recent development, what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

In a recent development, once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

Industry observers note that “Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a upcoming closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

Sources indicate that there’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

Industry News: A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he mentioned.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

According to recent reports, sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

It has been revealed that you have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

According to recent reports, what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

In a recent development, but you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

According to recent reports, often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

Industry observers note that but that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

In a recent development, and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré mentioned; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

A sprawling 8,300-square-foot hand-hewn log home on 22 wooded acres in Greenacres, WA has hit the market for under $3 million after a $320,000 price drop.

Built with full timber walls throughout and soaring views of the Pacific Northwest skyline, the seven-bedroom estate offers total seclusion just 15 minutes from the highway.

“It's huge. It's a 8,300-square-foot log cabin and the architecture on this one is just stunning. It's hand-hewn logs,” notes listing agent Denay Hornberger with Realty One Group Eclipse. “It’s a one-of-a-kind property and the owners added a bunch of beautiful features to it.”.

Completed in 2008, the sellers bought the place before it was completed and finished the construction.

According to recent reports, “When they first bought it, the builder had spent too much money building it and ended up having to sell it when it was half done. They came in and finished it and added hundreds of thousands of dollars to this property to make it what it is today.” Hornberger explains, adding she lives on an adjacent property. “With the money that's been put into it, [the sellers have] an eye for detail. I mean, everything about this home has been well thought out.”.

Now the owners are listing it for $2.875 million.

Industry observers note that “The thing about a property like this is trying to figure out exactly how to price it because there are no comps to really help you decide where the price is right,” she says, adding the initial asking price was a bit high. “I think we're now right in the sweet spot of where we need to be.”.

The home has seven bedrooms and seven bathrooms with real logs visible almost everywhere.

“There are similar log cabins but they're not fully log cabins the way that [this home] is. Sometimes you have little bits of logs and then you have drywall,” Hornberger states. “Here, the logs are everywhere throughout the house and that is extremely unique to have that. You feel like you are in a log cabin in every almost every single room you're in.”.

The fact the sellers spared no expense is evident immediately.

It has been revealed that “You walk in and your breath is just taken away. It is so beautiful and it's so grand that when you walk in, you just have to take a moment and appreciate it because the windows are huge, the logs are huge,” she says. “The fireplace is absolutely stunning, and then you look out the window to just woods and skyline. It's just stunning.”.

The home sits on 22-acres of land and while it seems far away from civilization, it isn’t.

Recent findings suggest that “You're actually 15 minutes from the freeway and you're about 20 minutes from the mall,” Hornberger says. “So even though you feel like you're in the middle of nowhere, you just drive a little bit and you're back in the mix of things. So, you get the best of both worlds.”.

It also epitomizes the feel of the Pacific Northwest.

It has been revealed that “We have that woodsy feel. People like to wear their flannel here and we're kind of a laid-back community,” she explains. “So [the house] is taking the best of the Pacific Northwest and having that cabin-in-the-woodsy feel, which is what we're known for.”.

The amount of land makes it perfect for outdoors activities like hiking and hunting, but the house is also luxurious, meaning two types of perfect buyers.

“If you just want to be outside, it’s a perfect home for that,” Hornberger says. “I think the second perfect buyer is somebody who wants a second home... who's in a hustle and bustle all the time but really wants that getaway that they can go to several times a year, have that peace and quiet from the city, get back to nature, and then go back to their regular lives at the end of the day.”.

#87743. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
📖 Baca

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that want to price more precisely?
  • Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

Sources indicate that A sold comp tells us where a buyer remarked yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

It has been revealed that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Sources indicate that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

In a recent development, it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

Recent findings suggest that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Recent findings suggest that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

In a recent development, this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

In a recent development, listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

According to recent reports, find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sources indicate that sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

Industry observers note that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.
