  • Industry observers note that A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov.
  • The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in New York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research said that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Industry observers note that A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in New York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research said that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

According to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

In a recent development, onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Manufacturer, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

According to recent reports, according to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs mentioned that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

Recent findings suggest that the plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under Fresh York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

They "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the Fresh York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

The case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins.".

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, stated that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them.".

Industry observers note that critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also stated that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russia has finally opened its crypto market for retail customers as its central bank today enabled trading in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for the general public.
  • The fresh regulation, unveiled by the Bank of Russia last week, took effect today, Nov.
  • Industry observers note that the announcement expands access to regulated crypto trading in the country and connects the assets with TradFi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russia has finally opened its crypto market for retail customers as its central bank today enabled trading in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for the general public. With the law signed by President Vladimir Putin, the Bank of Russia officially rolled out BTC, ETH, and USDT for public trading on domestic exchanges, beginning Nov. 17, 2026.

The fresh regulation, unveiled by the Bank of Russia last week, took effect today, Nov. 17. The move allows individual customers to purchase these assets through intermediaries, including brokers, exchanges, and authorized crypto marketplaces. This means ordinary investors can now buy up to 300,000 rubles ($3,700) in a year through a single broker, exchange, or asset manager, after passing a mandatory test.

Industry observers note that the announcement expands access to regulated crypto trading in the country and connects the assets with TradFi. This allows non-qualified investors to buy and trade BTC, ETH, and USDT directly through traditional exchanges and clearing systems.

However, qualified investors are not subject to such asset limits and trading restrictions.

The development points out that Russia has taken decisive action to deepen the integration of the crypto market with traditional finance. The debut indicates surging retail interest in cryptocurrency amid regulatory evolution.

It signals a strategic shift in how traditional exchanges handle digital assets. Accommodating retail clients signals growing confidence in the crypto market’s maturity. This highlights rising demand for coordinated exposure to crypto assets within Russia’s capital markets.

The announcement introduces latest entry gateways that give retail investors organized access to the crypto market, redefining how these assets are traded locally and internationally.

According to recent reports, in the past, crypto in Russia operated in a highly restrictive, complex regulatory environment. Now, the regulator is moving toward a balance between investor freedom and financial stability. In July, the central bank opened the door to crypto for companies to facilitate global trade. This month, it introduced new legislation that allows retail investors to trade crypto within specified limits.

Homebuilders’ $30B buying spree has cooled; now it’s all execution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for the better part of 15 years, U.S.
  • The buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals.
  • Recent findings suggest that yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for the better part of 15 years, U.S. homebuilding has been on a mergers-and-acquisitions buying spree. Since 2010, more than 200 homebuilder transactions have conservatively totaled more than $30 billion in declared deal value, based on just seven of the largest acquisitions and excluding scores of private-tech giant transactions whose purchase prices were never disclosed.

The buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals. More recent transactions included Daiwa House subsidiary Stanley Martin‘s July acquisition of Holiday Builders, Dream Finders Homes‘ August acquisition of Beazer Homes, and Century Communities’ October purchase of HistoryMaker Homes.

Recent findings suggest that yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted. Weak demand, costly sales incentives, shrinking margins, and uncertainty over land and home values are forcing acquirers to reconsider not only which businesses are worth buying but also how the companies they already own should operate.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re not busy now,” one deeply experienced homebuilding M&A dealmaker told me recently. “This is no time to be trying to take a seller to market for acquisition. Nothing’s happening.”.

According to recent reports, that assessment does not mean homebuilding consolidation has ended. It’s still “morning time in America” for homebuilding’s inevitable grind toward concentration of fewer, ever larger, more industrialized homebuilding giants.

My source’s observation suggests that the economics of bringing new sellers to market have become harder, even as the largest and best-capitalized acquirers continue pursuing strategic combinations.

Industry observers note that business and investment models in homebuilding can look remarkably good when demand, prices, and asset values are rising. The real test comes when the cycle turns, gravity takes hold, and assumptions that worked on the way up begin to break down. That’s when the industry’s outliers distinguish themselves, not simply through stronger balance sheets, but by how well their people work together, how quickly they adapt their processes, how effectively they serve customers, and how consistently they outperform competitors when business conditions get messy.

That is the test now confronting the companies assembled through homebuilding’s extraordinary consolidation era. Have their acquisitions produced merely bigger enterprises, or have they developed the leadership, operating discipline, local knowledge, and capacity to improve that will make them fundamentally better homebuilders with greater connectivity to and attainability for America’s economically bifurcated households?

According to recent reports, the answer will increasingly depend on what happens inside the enterprises they’ve acquired. The challenge is to capture the value of their land positions while developing the people, operating systems, technologies, and organizational capabilities needed to replenish those positions, improve profitability, and serve customers more efficiently in a difficult market likely to extend into 2027 and potentially 2028.

That is where the next, and perhaps most demanding, phase of homebuilding consolidation begins.

Homebuilding acquisitions are distinct from many other corporate combinations because the value of the acquired business is inseparable from its land positions and the people capable of turning those positions – sustainably and repeatedly – into profitable homes.

An attractive acquisition may bring years of controlled lots, entitled development opportunities, established relationships with landowners and municipalities, and access to markets that would take an outsider years to enter. It may also include an experienced management team, trusted trade relationships, established brands and the organizational knowledge and local intel needed to perpetuate the business beyond its current land pipeline.

Those assets are related, but they are not interchangeable. When one goes missing, the others promptly fall out of balance. The value of the land depends on its location, basis, development requirements, timing, and the demand for homes that can be built on it profitably. Realizing that value depends on decisions about product, construction costs, sales strategy, purchasing, development sequencing, and capital allocation.

In a recent development, an acquirer that buys a good land portfolio but loses the ability to develop and replenish it efficiently may find that the acquisition’s original promise was a mere blip. An acquirer that preserves an admired local management organization without improving its operating economics may find that the business remains well regarded yet increasingly uncompetitive.

Successful acquisitions require balancing those two realities. The objective is to capture the value of the acquired land and operating platform as a launching pad for building the leadership, relationships, systems, and financial discipline needed to extend that profitability long after the original inventory has been delivered.

That balance of 100% binding capabilities becomes harder to hold together when market conditions weaken.

For years, one of the most attractive features of selling to Berkshire Hathaway’s Clayton Properties Group or one of the major Japan-based acquirers was the prospect of continuity.

Recent findings suggest that many regional builders joined larger, well-capitalized ownership organizations while retaining key elements of their identities, management teams, local relationships, and operating independence. That approach appealed to owners seeking liquidity or a succession solution without losing the character of the companies they had built.

In a recent development, it also made strategic sense. Local knowledge, land relationships, management experience, customer trust, and an almost irreplicable entrepreneurial fire and come-what-may resiliency were among the assets the buyers sought to acquire.

In a recent development, but serving as a benevolent, deep-pocketed, and patient capital-access channel for a local autonomy confederation across an expanding collection of businesses comes at a cost. Separate purchasing organizations, technology systems, back-office functions, product-development practices, and management structures can limit the benefits of larger ownership. When sales are strong and margins are healthy, those costs may be easier to absorb. When sales slow, incentives rise, and profitability contracts, the economics become less forgiving.

According to recent reports, the pressure to coordinate operations, consolidate functions, standardize selected processes, and reduce unnecessary overhead intensifies. So do difficult decisions about regional leadership, divisional responsibilities, and the roles of managers at the divisional and neighborhood level who helped make the acquired businesses successful in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that those decisions can be disruptive, especially for employees and former owners who believed their companies would continue operating as they had before the acquisition and, in some cases, had enjoyed a solid few-year runway of exactly that. Some will regard the changes as evidence that the new parent does not understand the business it acquired. Others will see them as necessary steps toward strengthening the combined organization.

Eliminating management positions or consolidating administrative functions does not, by itself, demonstrate operational improvement. Nor does a departure from established practices necessarily indicate that an acquirer has made a strategic mistake or an unforced error.

The relevant test is whether the changes improve the organization’s ability to develop land, build homes, serve customers, maintain valuable relationships and generate returns that stakeholders and owners can count on as durable. That is a more useful standard than judging an acquisition by how many legacy executives remain in place or by how many familiar operating practices survive.

An key distinction exists among the companies driving the latest phase of consolidation. Daiwa House, Sekisui House, Sumitomo Forestry, and Berkshire Hathaway operate with strategic planning horizons and ownership structures that can offer greater flexibility than the quarter-to-quarter performance pressures faced by many publicly traded U.S. homebuilders.

In a recent development, the Japanese companies are publicly traded, and Berkshire Hathaway is accountable to its shareholders. None is insulated from financial performance requirements. But their diversified businesses, substantial resources, and long-term commitments to housing and related industries can allow them to invest in capabilities whose returns may take years to materialize.

So far, that difference has played out as an “acquirer-of-choice” factor as homebuilding firm sellers considered how firms organize and develop the businesses they acquire.

Industry observers note that A longer-term ownership philosophy does not require codifying every management position or maintaining every regional operating structure indefinitely. In fact, patient capital may be most valuable when it enables an organization to undertake difficult transformations without expecting every investment to deliver an immediate earnings benefit.

The challenge is to distinguish costs that can be eliminated from capabilities that need strengthening.

Industry observers note that japan-based companies also have another potentially important advantage. Their experience with industrialized construction, standardized components, manufacturing systems, production engineering and deeply vertical integration extends well beyond what is typical of conventional American site-built homebuilding.

Clayton also brings experience in manufactured housing, factory-based production, and vertically integrated housing-related businesses. Its expanding site-built platform, particularly following the Taylor Morrison acquisition, creates opportunities to combine capabilities that have historically operated in unrelated realms of the residential construction business.

Recent findings suggest that none of this means that industrialized methods developed elsewhere can simply be transplanted into American site-built construction. Differences in building codes, product preferences, transportation, trade labor, land development, and construction practices remain unsolved obstacles.

It has been revealed that the industry has not yet demonstrated that these capabilities can be deployed broadly enough to transform the economics of conventional site-built housing. Still, the long-term strategic opportunity is hard to refute.

A collection of independently operated regional builders can provide market presence, land access, local expertise and “trust capital.” A more coordinated enterprise may also provide the common systems, product architecture, production volumes, and organizational learning needed to adapt industrialized methods across multiple markets.

According to recent reports, as ambitions go, that’s far bigger than reducing SG&A. It also raises a question that applies to every major acquirer: Which capabilities should remain local, which should be shared across the enterprise, and which should be fundamentally reengineered into the holistic, interoperable system modern homebuilding organizations seem to need?

According to recent reports, homebuilding has long featured an argument over whether privately held regional builders are inherently better businesses than their larger public competitors. The case for private builders emphasizes their closeness to customers, knowledge of local land markets, relationships with municipalities and trades, and the loyalty and committed engagement of talented employees who have worked together for years.

According to recent reports, those advantages are real in many companies. They can influence everything from land acquisition opportunities to construction execution and customer referrals. But private ownership does not guarantee those qualities, just as public or institutional ownership does not necessarily diminish them.

A privately held firm can become inefficient, undercapitalized, or resistant to change. A large enterprise can cultivate strong local leadership, build trusted community relationships, and adopt operating practices that improve the customer experience.

The more useful distinction concerns the quality of the operating organization, a characteristic we’ve talked about as homebuilding’s “outlier” factor.

Industry observers note that does it put decisions in the hands of people with the knowledge to make them? Does it give those people the resources, information, and accountability to perform effectively? Can it identify successful practices and extend their benefits beyond the division where they originated?

Answers to those questions reveal more than public or private ownership labels. They also help explain why the integration decisions now confronting the major consolidators are so difficult. An organization can destroy valuable local capabilities by centralizing too much. It can also waste substantial resources and miss opportunities to improve by centralizing too little.

Recent findings suggest that integration is knowing the difference. Some acquirers are good integrators. That doesn’t mean people swept up in them, or spat out due to them, agree.

According to recent reports, for decades, scale in homebuilding has largely meant more closings, more communities, more controlled lots, greater geographic reach, and increased purchasing power that leads to market-share advantages. Those advantages remain as a bulwark of near-flywheel-like value creation. Larger builders can spread fixed costs across more homes, negotiate favorable supplier arrangements, diversify market exposure, and access capital on terms that smaller competitors may struggle to match.

Still, everyone who’s done well in the business can attest that size alone does not explain why some organizations consistently outperform others.

It has been revealed that A more meaningful definition of scale includes an enterprise’s ability to combine capital, land, local knowledge, talent, technology, and relationships into an operating system that continuously improves performance. In that sense, homebuilding was AI before AI was cool because its best operators knew and practiced “recursive learning” as a core skill set.

Industry observers note that that means acquiring land at bases that support acceptable returns under realistic demand assumptions. It also means developing products that customers value without unnecessary design, material, or construction complexity.

It means coordinating suppliers and trades to reduce delays, rework, and waste. It also means developing managers who can exercise sound judgment locally while drawing on the organization’s broader capabilities. It also means using information gathered across markets to make better decisions throughout the enterprise.

A builder operating in 20 markets should have opportunities to learn from 20 distinct sets of customers, land conditions, construction challenges, and operating practices. But those opportunities yield little advantage if the information remains trapped within individual divisions or if the organization lacks the discipline to identify and transfer improvements.

Recent findings suggest that this is where AI-powered data systems and other technology capabilities could change the economics of scale. Better demand forecasting, more accurate construction scheduling, earlier detection of cost overruns, improved land underwriting, and more systematic comparisons of product performance could help organizations spot problems sooner and make decisions faster.

AI could help reveal patterns that managers would otherwise struggle to recognize in large volumes of operational data. It could also make institutional knowledge more accessible to those making daily decisions about land, purchasing, construction, and sales.

But value will not come from installing technology alone. Companies will need reliable data, consistent definitions, disciplined operating processes, and managers who can distinguish useful insights from misleading conclusions. They will also need to recognize that an approach that works in one market may be a fool’s errand in another.

Sources indicate that competitive advantage will belong to organizations that can repeatedly measure performance, understand what drives it, test improvements, and incorporate what they learn into their operating practices. That is how scale becomes a capability rather than merely a measurement of size.

The difficult market conditions facing builders through 2027, and potentially into 2028, will make these distinctions more apparent. Management teams will face pressure to reduce overhead, preserve liquidity, reassess land commitments, control construction costs, and improve returns on capital. Some will need to reorganize divisions, consolidate functions, or change leadership.

Sources indicate that the companies that emerge stronger will not necessarily be the ones that make the deepest cuts. They will be the ones that understand which costs can be eliminated without harming the business and which investments are necessary to improve its future performance. That requires financial discipline, but it also requires patience, sound leadership judgment, and a willingness to challenge established practices.

It has been revealed that it may require replacing an operating system that has worked adequately for years. It may also mean changing the responsibilities of respected executives or asking local teams to adopt practices developed elsewhere in the enterprise.

It may also require resisting the temptation to standardize activities that rely on local relationships and judgment. The objective should be neither to preserve acquired companies exactly as they were nor to eliminate their differences in pursuit of corporate uniformity.

It should be to develop organizations that can achieve what their constituent businesses could not accomplish independently.

In a recent development, the returns earned by companies that participated in homebuilding’s consolidation era will not reflect the ultimate opportunity. American homebuilding remains a uniquely complex process of converting land, capital, materials, labor, knowledge, and time into a finished product that households can purchase. Every unnecessary delay, redundant process, avoidable error, excessive handoff, and poorly coordinated decision adds cost somewhere along that process.

Some of those costs are so sticky they seem almost unavoidable. Others reflect operating practices that have persisted through the decades because the industry has struggled to coordinate the many participants involved in building a home.

Larger enterprises with better information, stronger leadership, deeper technical capabilities, and greater capacity to invest in improvement can change that.

The goal should be a homebuilding value stream that produces more value with less wasted time, effort, and expense, i.e., less “stream.”.

Recent findings suggest that better execution will not, by itself, overcome high land prices, expensive financing, restrictive regulation, infrastructure constraints, or the gap between household incomes and housing costs. Those barriers remain substantial. But homebuilders have meaningful control over how they organize their businesses and how efficiently they turn resources into finished homes.

Recent findings suggest that the industry’s era of consolidation has brought together an enormous collection of land assets, operating organizations, local relationships, and management talent under larger ownership platforms. What happens next will determine whether those combinations yield more than additional market share and purchasing leverage.

The most notable measure of homebuilding’s great acquisition era may ultimately have little to do with how many companies changed hands or how much their buyers paid.

It may be how much better those enterprises become at converting land, capital, talent, and knowledge into homes that more American households can afford.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a upcoming CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no looks to change that.” He mentioned he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

It has been revealed that consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based manufacturer acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and claims it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Sources indicate that zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the tech giant.

Industry observers note that zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but noted Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 upcoming customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the firm’s 2026 initiative, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli stated.

In a recent development, zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli mentioned Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the significant players.”.

According to recent reports, consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

Industry observers note that “Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lionel Fermin examines when growing businesses may need technology leadership for planning, security, spending, and long-term technology decisions.

HOBBS, N.M., Nov. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When does a business need a Fractional CIO? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin of GlobaTech Solutions in Hobbs, New Mexico, explains when businesses may benefit from experienced technology leadership.

The HelloNation article explains that technology decisions often become more complicated as a business grows. New employees, software, equipment, and security risks can create challenges that basic technical support may not address. At that point, business leaders may need broader guidance about how technology supports the organization.

Industry observers note that the article describes a Fractional CIO as someone who provides technology leadership without serving as a full-time executive. While technical support typically focuses on fixing problems and keeping systems working, this role considers how technology decisions affect employees, customers, security, costs, and future business needs.

This broader perspective can become important when several technology projects compete for attention. The article notes that businesses may recognize the need for improvements without knowing which ones should come first. Fractional CIO services can help prioritize projects according to risk, cost, and business value.

Technology planning is another major part of the role. Instead of waiting for systems or equipment to fail, the article explains that companies can prepare for equipment replacements, software changes, security improvements, and growth. Identifying major expenses early can also give leaders more time to compare options and prepare budgets.

Cybersecurity can create another need for technology leadership. The article notes that a security incident can interrupt operations, create financial losses, and affect customer relationships. Executive technology guidance can help leaders understand cybersecurity risks in business terms and determine which concerns deserve the most attention.

Industry observers note that the article also describes how Fractional CIO services can assist with customer or industry security requirements. Businesses may receive questionnaires or requests to demonstrate specific protections. Technology leadership can help identify gaps, organize responses, and provide a clearer view of existing security practices.

Recent findings suggest that growth can also signal the need for more structured technology guidance. Systems that worked for a small team may become strained as a organization adds employees. The article explains that a technology strategy can help businesses prepare for greater demands on software, networks, security, and employee access.

According to recent reports, vendor management is another area where stronger oversight may be useful. Companies often work with separate providers for software, internet service, phones, security, and technical support. The article notes that reviewing vendor costs, contracts, performance, and responsibilities can help reduce duplication and clarify who handles important technology needs.

According to recent reports, major business changes can also increase the need for planning. Opening a new office, replacing software, or hiring many employees may require coordination among leadership, employees, vendors, and technical teams. Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin's insights featured in the article address how technology leadership can help keep these decisions connected to broader company goals.

Sources indicate that the article notes that not every firm needs a full-time technology executive. Smaller businesses may instead need experienced guidance for certain projects or a limited number of hours. Warning signs can include rising technology costs, repeated cybersecurity concerns, unsuccessful projects, or leaders spending too much time managing technology questions.

Sources indicate that A lack of shared planning may provide another warning sign. When departments make separate technology decisions, businesses can face higher costs, security gaps, and software problems. The article explains that a shared technology strategy can provide clearer direction across the organization.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the article explains that the value of a Fractional CIO centers on planning and leadership rather than daily troubleshooting. Strong technology guidance can help businesses organize decisions about systems, security, spending, growth, and long-term needs.

When a Business Needs a Fractional CIO features insights from Lionel Fermin, Managed IT Expert of Hobbs, Upcoming Mexico, in HelloNation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple-backed XRP treasury tech giant Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

As per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

According to recent reports, evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the tech giant is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

In a recent development, for reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

In a recent development, the recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

Sources indicate that on Oct. 14, Evernorth announced collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.

Tech Report: Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%.
  • It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through.
  • I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives?

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that’s not what’s happening.

I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline.

Recent findings suggest that oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off. Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t.

In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members said anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money.

Sources indicate that in any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we announced a deal with Iran in June.

In a recent development, I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing issues, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the company’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was announced.

The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune.

It has been revealed that if we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama.

Sources indicate that for the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let’s take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren’t lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks.

It has been revealed that the Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates.

Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.
  • But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move.
  • The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration initiative and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

It has been revealed that the technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository states a yes vote does two things:.

Industry observers note that it also claims plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

In a recent development, A no vote would stop the whole strategy. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 indicated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Sources indicate that turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Industry observers note that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

According to recent reports, the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

It has been revealed that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

Industry observers note that the spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

In a recent development, at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Recent findings suggest that proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence indicates what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

Recent findings suggest that the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the strategy goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.
  • The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software tech giant, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

According to recent reports, his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health prepares that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their aims “after we’ve built our product.”.

Industry observers note that but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

In a recent development, “Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it indicates.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site states, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Sources indicate that kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend mentioned I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman remarked the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”.

The Sojourn site says the manufacturer is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native tech giant in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn aims to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

A fresh health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the firm hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

It has been revealed that kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He remarked at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

Bank of America has disclosed a position in an XRP exchange-traded fund in its latest quarterly 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, dated Nov. 16, shows that the bank held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI), worth about $106,600, at the end of the third quarter.

It has been revealed that bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

Seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed the largest stake among them, at $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a fresh position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million.

In a recent development, UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Most of the UBS position was in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, and Morgan Stanley held funds from Franklin, REX-Osprey and Bitwise.

In a recent development, JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $9,000, and National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the same fund, worth about $5,500. Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

Recent findings suggest that the crypto portfolio of Goldman Sachs grew to $2.64 billion by the end of September, according to its 13F filing. The bank held about $1.28 billion in Bitcoin ETFs, and BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC accounted for $778 million and $398 million of that amount, respectively. Goldman also held about $1.22 billion in Ether funds, and BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $603 million of that amount.

Goldman held $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from $87 million at the end of the second quarter. The bank's 13F filing for the first quarter indicated no XRP or Solana ETF holdings, and Goldman still held no Solana funds at the end of September.

The bank held shares of five spot XRP funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its Franklin Templeton position was worth almost $48 million.

Besides, trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP funds, and Simplex Trading disclosed a $14 million stake in the Grayscale fund. EP Wealth Advisors raised its Volatility Shares XRP ETF holding by 37% to 18,400 shares, worth about $148,000.

According to recent reports, A 13F filing only shows long positions as of Sept. 30. It doesn't show whether the banks hedge those holdings with shorts, or what they did with the shares in October and November. Since then, XRP has fallen below $1, and on Tuesday morning, XRP was trading at $0.966.

Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries.
  • companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:50 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier.

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In a recent development, in this episode we examine the challenges around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:.

According to recent reports, first, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:.

Sources indicate that the first set of takeaways from our survey indicates a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

In a recent development, as shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

Industry observers note that as seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer says deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

It’s early days, so some customers are waiting for clearer sovereign-specific mandates or enforcement guidelines from local governments before expanding deployment and testing sovereignty. In other words, they’re leaning on existing privacy and cybersecurity laws and practices. We’d caution, however, that this type of uncertainty only strengthens the case for preparing acceptance tests sooner rather than later.

According to recent reports, costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision. At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

Industry observers note that AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

According to recent reports, google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

In a recent development, now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:.

Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Let’s dig into some more survey data.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Recent findings suggest that under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Sources indicate that customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

It has been revealed that coming back to the AI inference issue. As we highlighted earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract notes.”.

This means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

For sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

It has been revealed that sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

Industry observers note that in this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:.

Industry observers note that we see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

Sources indicate that this means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

According to recent reports, for vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

Sources indicate that sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

Will the AI stock sell-off give us sub-7% mortgage rates before the holidays?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu!
  • In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:.
  • Industry observers note that if all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates?

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:.

Industry observers note that if all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%.Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed’s hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there?1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable.2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war.3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently.We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher.

In a recent development, mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a substantial variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads’ job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

Sources indicate that we saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today.Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:.

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:.

Sources indicate that housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time.

Inventory growth is running at 8.12%.

New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June, and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since early 2022. One concern always with higher rates is that sellers will decide not to put their homes on the market; that has not happened this year, which is a positive sign for housing.In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:.

Industry observers note that typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point, demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%, and last week the year-over-year price-cut gap was 2% higher than last year when demand was picking up with lower rates.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast is going to have a hard time being right this year. I simply don’t have enough time to be correct, as most of the year prices have been rising roughly 1%-2 % with the Case-Shiller Index. It’s only recently that we can see some negative year-over-year data, and we only have a few weeks left in the year.The price-cut percentage for last week:.

It’s Thanksgiving week, so this means we can see some crazy volatility with stocks and bonds — and some hours with not a lot of volume. Next week’s tracker will obviously be hit by the holidays. However, this week we do have some economic data that can move the markets. PCE inflation, new home sales, PMI and other reports will add to the mix of volatility. And who knows what “upgrades” might shut down another institution or part of our infrastructure from operating normally this week!
