💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.
  • According to recent reports, companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data.
  • The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.

According to recent reports, companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology.

The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.

Recent findings suggest that the funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession.

Sources indicate that the numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data highlights. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025.

The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents.

Industry observers note that the biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models.

Recent findings suggest that customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation.

Recent findings suggest that among companies focused on AI-generated speech, Newly introduced York-based ElevenLabs unveiled a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The organization is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing.

Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July.

It has been revealed that voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders.

In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology.

The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean company behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21.

Looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram unveiled looks to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework.

More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end.

Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.”.

After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he noted.

In a recent development, bitcoin's 200-week moving average (200WMA) has climbed above $68,000 for the first time, Blockstream CEO Adam Back noted on X on Nov. 18. "Bitcoin passes $68k 200wma," he wrote. Back attached a 200-week moving average heatmap from Look Into Bitcoin, and the chart highlights the indicator rising throughout Bitcoin's history. On Nov. 18, the indicator was between $67,955 and $68,145.

#bitcoin passes $68k 200wma https://t.co/dgIzS9Nsvw https://t.co/xzYdP0EvZh.

Back is the cryptographer behind Hashcash. The algorithm laid the groundwork for proof-of-work, and Satoshi Nakamoto cited it in the Bitcoin white paper. Back was also one of the first people Satoshi contacted before the launch of Bitcoin in 2009.

The Blockstream CEO has posted about the 200WMA on X several times this year. On March 27, he wrote that the "200wma passes $59k." The indicator was just above $60,000 in early May, and on May 30, Back reported that it had crossed $61,000. In September, the 200WMA rose above $65,000 for the first time.

Sources indicate that in a follow-up post in May, Back cited a maxim of the late Charlie Munger. According to Munger, an investor who buys only high-quality assets when they trade at the 200-week moving average would beat the S&P 500 over time. Back also noted that Munger and Warren Buffett never embraced Bitcoin.

In mid-September, Bitcoin was trading at around $76,000 to $77,000. At that time, the gap between the price and the 200WMA was more than $10,000.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday, Bitcoin was trading at $64,150, about 6% below the 200WMA. On Nov. 15, BTC dropped as low as $62,000 before bouncing 5.5%. Back called the move "bouncy" in a post on X.

In a CNBC interview on Nov. 12, Back remarked that Bitcoin could reach $1 million by 2028. According to Back, more than 95% of potential institutional inflows into Bitcoin are still ahead. He named investment trusts, asset managers and corporate treasuries among the buyers, and he said that their buying was just beginning.

According to recent reports, back also pointed to the Bitcoin halving in the spring of 2028. He said that miners would sell fewer coins after it.

He made a similar point at Paris Blockchain Week in April. "When the Bitcoin price is low, the miners have to sell a bigger proportion… and when the price is higher, they don't have to sell as much," Back remarked at the time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.
  • Sources indicate that sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Sources indicate that panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sources indicate that sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company prepares to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Sources indicate that panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, stated Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

It has been revealed that “This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

In a recent development, batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

It has been revealed that berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

It has been revealed that in August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

In a recent development, the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

According to recent reports, the organization has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round declared in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

In a recent development, group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently confirmed aims for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he noted.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

Sources indicate that “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky remarked. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • According to recent reports, one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • Recent findings suggest that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path highlights how far the probing went.

According to recent reports, one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Recent findings suggest that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, states user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

Sources indicate that the loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction reveals a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

It has been revealed that that arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

Industry observers note that the harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 revision named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale indicates its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Industry observers note that loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

Sources indicate that the two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

According to recent reports, the takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

Sources indicate that this looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem reveals pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

Recent findings suggest that on the Nov. 14 episode of Saturday Night Live, host John Mulaney starred in a parody drug ad for “Sister,” “a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.”.

It has been revealed that the sketch spread across social media within days, largely because so many viewers saw their own families in it. Its jokes land on real pressure points in American caregiving: who does the work, what it costs them, and how much more of it is coming.

A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans, nearly 1 in 4 adults, had provided ongoing care in the past year to an adult or child with a medical condition or disability. That is 45% more caregivers than a decade earlier.

The work has also gotten harder. More than 40% of caregivers provide high-intensity care, and more than half perform medical and nursing tasks such as giving injections and managing catheters. Only 22% have been trained to do them.

According to recent reports, an aging population is the main driver, says Geoff Gross, founder and CEO of Medical Guardian, a Philadelphia-based medical alert and connected-care tech giant. But strains on the broader care system are pushing more Americans into the role.

“What we’re also seeing is pressures on in-home care and labor overall,” Gross mentioned. “There’s a burden on caregivers right now that is not scalable.”.

Industry observers note that paid help is scarce and expensive. As gerontologists Jane Tavares and Marc Cohen wrote for Fortune, a home health aide runs a median of about $6,688 a month, while the direct care workforce remains underpaid and short-staffed.

The sketch opens with Mulaney’s character weighing a nursing home against a private aide who “could cost thousands a week.” For real families, the costs keep compounding long after the caregiving ends.

In a recent development, A report published Nov. 4 by the AARP Public Policy Institute modeled the lifetime income losses of working caregivers born between 1981 and 1985. The typical caregiver in that group stands to lose about $120,500 in earnings, workplace retirement income, and Social Security, including roughly $15,400 in retirement and Social Security income alone.

Across that single five-year birth cohort, the losses add up to an estimated $2.3 trillion. Only 3.4% of working caregivers in the model lost no work hours to care. Chandra Bozelko, who cares full-time for her parents, ran those numbers on her own family in a recent Fortune commentary.

Industry observers note that for some, the strain reaches the basics. In the 2025 AARP survey, 1 in 5 caregivers said they couldn’t afford necessities such as food.

The sketch’s sharpest line comes from a doctor, played by Mikey Day, who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours.”.

Research from the University of Michigan published in October suggests the gap behind the joke is widening. If current rates hold, U.S. women can expect to spend seven years of their lives caring for older family members or friends, up from six in 2011. Men’s lifetime total held steady at four.

It has been revealed that the difference isn’t in caring for spouses, where men and women spend about the same time. It indicates up in care for parents and grandparents. Edward Jones managing partner Penny Pennington has called it “the elder daughter phenomenon,” arguing that eldest daughters are quietly propping up family finances.

“Women still bear disproportionate financial burden, time burden, and energy burden,” Gross mentioned, adding that any progress on the glitch “isn’t happening fast enough.”.

In a recent development, demand for care will only grow. The U.S. Census Bureau projects that in 2029, Americans 65 and older will outnumber those under 18.

“Caregiving is really a societal crisis, but it isn’t designated in that way as much as it should be compared to other things we read about each and every day,” Gross said.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (891 w)

What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations.
  • The limitations have been understood for some time.
  • In a recent development, for founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business?

The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it revealed how much weight public markets now place on a single private organization’s numbers.

In a recent development, for founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing.

In a recent development, ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting.

Industry observers note that the first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month.

Industry observers note that what gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts.

According to recent reports, companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable.

It has been revealed that take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter.

These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that.

In a recent development, if a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size.

In a recent development, later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises.

In a recent development, retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked.

ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon.

What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could.

Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to organization building with founders.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle tech giant talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle tech giant talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

Sources indicate that “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the firm’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”.

Industry observers note that the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy noted there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the manufacturer in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The latest products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

Recent findings suggest that “Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

Industry observers note that AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy stated. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The upcoming products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Sources indicate that plenty of organization: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he stated.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy mentioned.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the organization’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

Recent findings suggest that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy mentioned. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy remarked Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy mentioned, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

It has been revealed that about 40 of the firm’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy remarked Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building newly introduced products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the organization, Duffy mentioned Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy remarked Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • MEXC says user assets remain secure.
  • On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

According to recent reports, MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange claims it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, looks to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN states the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

It has been revealed that the charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN indicates MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

It has been revealed that iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

Industry observers note that the order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

According to recent reports, section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

In a recent development, one provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

In a recent development, for most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

It has been revealed that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

It has been revealed that predicting how consumers or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta employees have raised concerns about the organization’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters.
  • In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.
  • Industry observers note that “This seems like an extreme privacy violation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have raised concerns about the organization’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters.

In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.

Industry observers note that “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted.

A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported.

Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.”.

In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating due to built-in prompts that were designed to engage owners between sessions, according to Reuters.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he remarked, adding that other cases involved “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”.

The random, out-of-context messages were confirmed as hallucinations.

A Meta spokesperson said employee testing is core to product development and is meant to generate feedback in order to implement privacy safeguards, adding that employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public does and that some functions aren’t available elsewhere.

As for the Muse messages that referred to encrypted Signal chats, the spokesperson pointed out that Android owners have the option to grant apps notification access, which they must opt in to and is not specific to Muse.

“With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on,” Meta explained.

Since Muse was rolled out in September, it’s been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to the social-media giant’s blueprint to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI.

It has been revealed that but other companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents. For example, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon noted the bank won’t allow agents to access customer accounts and act on their behalf.

Similarly, Amazon won’t let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is already fighting to keep out Perplexity’s AI agents.

The process of raising those barriers, however, also entails network upgrades that may be contributing to a sudden surge in outages.

In recent weeks, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, Apple, and Microsoft saw temporary service disruptions. U.S. officials have mentioned there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting software patches were deployed before all the bugs were worked out.

Industry observers note that because AI tools can find vulnerabilities faster than companies can safely fix them, the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed, Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times.

In an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent firm Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.

In a recent development, “This is a substantial blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he said. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”.

Breaking: Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Industry observers note that for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale.
  • A firm can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A firm can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

According to recent reports, venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Industry observers note that institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Industry observers note that founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an crucial regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

As an example, Pear Therapeutics revealed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

It has been revealed that early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Sources indicate that has the founder or tech giant addressed these problems in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

Industry observers note that these challenges make the earliest stages of company formation particularly vital. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the tech giant is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

That means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

It has been revealed that AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

It has been revealed that the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

It has been revealed that moving rapidly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

For investors, the lesson is equally key — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a company needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

Recent findings suggest that the most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

According to recent reports, for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Trump administration has insisted that the recent surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure.

Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.

One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.

According to recent reports, “There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”.

FEMA didn’t respond to a request for comment.

It has been revealed that even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already on edge after the Pentagon introduced an initiative called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

Recent findings suggest that then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.” The Nvidia spy scandal also didn’t help sentiment.

Sources indicate that last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.

Industry observers note that days later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves.

Industry observers note that U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch newly uncovered vulnerabilities were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”.

Sources indicate that despite the administration’s denials that cybersecurity was an concern, the White House removed U.S. National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday. CNN also reported Friday that noted the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database—the second such breach in recent months.

The steady drumbeat of alarming news has pushed many Americans into panic mode. Costco and Walmart have seen more shoppers stocking up on emergency supplies.

“Consumer anxiety, following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media, have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco,” Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a recent note.

Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.

And for good measure, the stock market has been pummeled with some of the worst declines since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic as investors fear the end of the AI boom could take the U.S. economy down with it.

The cumulative effect of all the disruptions has caused Americans to fear the worst. Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press last week “there’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack.

“We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”.

But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, noted there’s nothing linking the outages.

In a recent development, “This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite swiftly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”.

Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten.
  • Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he noted, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

Industry observers note that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

In a recent development, I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

It has been revealed that revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in latest customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Sources indicate that entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying fresh things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Industry observers note that take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a significant deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Sources indicate that look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

Industry observers note that I love setting goals. I’m a big believer in having a vision and building a proposal to get there. I’ve also learned that a new calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

It has been revealed that you don’t have to overhaul the whole company all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

It has been revealed that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a tech giant.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

Latest Update: SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text.
  • Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft.
  • The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets states it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

In a recent development, that delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

It has been revealed that review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule highlights up in a White House queue.

Industry observers note that "Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record claims what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

In a recent development, rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Recent findings suggest that existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency looks for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

In a recent development, commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Industry observers note that rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Recent findings suggest that crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

Sources indicate that the sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

It has been revealed that the package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.
