📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation company?

Shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was currently on the market.

“I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation firm at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe says in a upcoming interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

It has been revealed that in 1992, Shawe and his business partner, Liz Elting, co-founded TransPerfect from his NYU dorm room. They didn’t have a large financial backer underwriting their ambitions. They financed the business themselves, leaned on credit cards and tried to find customers.

First, the founders had to persuade someone to hire them.

“We would basically cold-call till our fingers bled,” Shawe notes.

They also faxed prospects and sent mailers containing information and brochures. As projects came in, they built a network of linguists to handle the work. Shawe’s description of the early sales strategy is simple: “Brute force clients in the door.”.

In a recent development, shawe has since helped turn that operation into a business generating $1.32 billion in annual revenue. He notes that TransPerfect now has more than 10,000 employees, whose work extends from translating contracts and supporting global drug studies to developing software and helping companies implement AI.

Shawe states that about half of the company’s revenue still comes from language translation services. The rest comes from technology consulting and other businesses shaped around customer needs.

Industry observers note that as TransPerfect has grown, so has Shawe’s net worth. According to the Forbes billionaires list, Shawe, 57, is right now worth $1.7 billion.

According to recent reports, transPerfect produced about $400,000 in revenue in its first year, Shawe claims. He recalls that the manufacturer broke even that year, with little choice but to keep spending below what it brought in.

It has been revealed that the founders reinvested in the company as it grew. There was an exception to the largely self-financed approach: In 1998, Shawe claims, they separated the technology business from the traditional translation operation and raised $4.1 million, with Deutsche Bank as the lead investor.

In a recent development, after the internet bubble burst, he and his partner used their own money to return investors’ original capital. Shawe later bought out his partner in 2018.

Sources indicate that shawe does not credit the tech giant’s rise entirely to persistence. TransPerfect arrived as the internet and globalization created upcoming connections across borders. The founders worked hard, but the timing helped.

In a recent development, however, as the company expanded, landing work was not the toughest problem. Shawe indicates hiring and retaining people who could deliver the work became harder. The founders could not oversee every project or client relationship, so training employees became increasingly vital.

Growth also taught Shawe a costly lesson about the difference between a customer’s promise and a binding commitment.

According to recent reports, early on, a client indicated that a substantial amount of business was coming. TransPerfect opened an Atlanta office, placed people on-site and made significant investments to prepare. Then the customer changed course, leaving the company financially exposed.

“It almost put us out of business,” Shawe indicates.

Sources indicate that he says that situation was his most expensive mistake as a founder. The error was investing heavily in a venture without adequate contractual protection. His takeaway was not to make massive capital commitments for business that a customer has only verbally agreed to provide.

Industry observers note that transPerfect started with cold outreach. Keeping customers helped it scale. “If you want a business to grow, the most vital thing you can do is retain your customers,” Shawe indicates.

Industry observers note that for TransPerfect, that meant hitting deadlines and delivering projects in the formats clients expect. Consistently performing well could turn a customer contact into an internal advocate, or someone willing to recommend the company to another team or division.

According to recent reports, shawe states referrals between divisions of large corporations is an key source of business. TransPerfect prefers to obtain fresh customers through recommendations from within an organization, and much of its sales activity now involves expanding services for existing customers.

TransPerfect also organized around industries. Once it had enough banking work, for example, it could build a dedicated finance division staffed with people who understood that sector. It applied the same approach to law firms, life sciences and luxury brands.

The company’s goal is to become a trusted advisor, not simply a supplier accepting translation orders. Listening to customers opened doors. For example, legal translation clients needed help with electronic discovery, or finding and processing digital information for litigation. TransPerfect expanded into those services, and Shawe notes the e-discovery and litigation-support business is on pace to generate $160 million or more this year.

“E-discovery and litigation support is not something that we started in the dorm room, but over the years enough of our customers communicated to us that they needed better or different services in this field, and that’s what drew us into it,” Shawe says.

He added that the business is now a “huge contributor” to the firm’s annual revenue.

TransPerfect faces latest advancements like AI and rapid translation features from tech giants like Apple and Google. Shawe says that TransPerfect must bring new technology to customers.

“We want to be the ones constantly disrupting our own business,” he says.

Shawe has witnessed several waves of technology reshape translation, including neural machine translation, or AI that automatically translates text with advanced technology, and now large language models, or AI programs trained on massive amounts of text data. Shawe says each change has created ways to accomplish more with fewer resources.

He notes that if formatting a multilingual manual once required 40 hours, and software can reduce that work to an hour or 15 minutes, TransPerfect should introduce the software, even if it loses billable hours.

“It might decrease our revenue in the short term, but it’s going to cement our client relationship and allow us to grow the business with that customer in the long term,” Shawe indicates.

TransPerfect can go beyond translating words and help businesses use language technology effectively. Shawe says customers continue to turn to the company for additional languages and higher-risk content even as automation handles more work.

He advises young founders to “raise as little money as possible” and “show real revenues as much as you can.”.

If he were starting from scratch with limited money and no network, he says he would focus on building relationships with customers and team members.

“These contacts that you make when you’re young, they compound like interest, and the value of those relationships also compounds,” Shawe states.

Shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was right now on the market.

Industry News: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Shows Us Why

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant.
  • According to recent reports, we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model.
  • Industry observers note that the SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value.

According to recent reports, we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a tech giant that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it.

Industry observers note that the SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value.

This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal.

The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked.

When OpenAI debuted ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025.

Recent findings suggest that the market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal.

From there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year.

In a recent development, as an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others.

Industry observers note that there were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole.

It has been revealed that that is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April.

It has been revealed that at my firm, Oxx, we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back.

In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike, whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October.

According to recent reports, the knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash.

It produced the unintended consequence of driving company ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value.

The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private organization transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem.

Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx, a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really significant step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Industry observers note that zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles mentioned.

It has been revealed that boles noted the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

According to recent reports, retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

In a recent development, next year, Zeno Power prepares to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

In a recent development, the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The organization is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

According to recent reports, since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The manufacturer has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. In a recent development, the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) on Nov. 18 with seven recommendations on the draft documents CP26/36 and GC26/7. Three of them concern CP26/36, and four concern GC26/7. The letter was signed by HPC chief executive Jake Chervinsky.

Recent findings suggest that the UK's newly introduced crypto regime will start to apply on Oct. 25, 2027. The FCA opened its window for crypto license applications on Sept. 30, 2026, and the window will close on Feb. 28, 2027.

According to the letter, "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity." HPC argued that attaching obligations to a person who could not discharge them "would offer consumers no additional protection.".

In the letter, HPC also compared public blockchains with the internet. "Like a public blockchain, the internet depends on protocols that identifiable persons maintain and upgrade over time," the group wrote.

It has been revealed that HPC asked the FCA to assess each participant in a blockchain network separately. Proprietary traders and market makers "supply much of the liquidity on which order books depend," the group wrote. HPC also asked the regulator to describe compliance requirements as outcomes and to hold regulated firms accountable for them.

It has been revealed that on Aug. 24, HPC urged the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to harmonize their rules for perpetual contracts. The group argued that such products should be classified by their economic structure. According to HPC, a harmonized framework would let exchanges compete on "execution quality and liquidity.".

In a recent development, on Sept. 30, HPC sent its response to the European Union's review of the MiCA rules. In it, the group asked the EU to treat crypto perpetual futures as derivatives under MiFID II. "Clarity in application, rather than upcoming legislation, is what would assist in regulating perpetual futures," HPC wrote at the time.

Latest Update: Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SlowMist indicates five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • It has been revealed that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist indicates five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

It has been revealed that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

It has been revealed that the reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis states had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery initiative has been confirmed.

Sources indicate that the design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

Sources indicate that the Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a upcoming wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most key fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

The lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Owners with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Want to Write Your First Novel? Here Are 10 Books to Read Before Picking Up Your Pen.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about.
  • So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it.
  • In a recent development, before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this upcoming world.

So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

In a recent development, before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

Then there’s the ending. How does an ending feel both surprising and inevitable?

The following 10 books offer a place to explore those questions. Some explain how to build a plot or develop a character. Others help you manage doubt and pay attention. They all treat fiction as a craft you can study. They can also keep you company as you begin writing a story of your own and remind you that you are not alone in your pursuit of writing a novel.

On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft.

It has been revealed that author Stephen King has published over 60 novels and sold more than 350 million copies of his books globally. In this book, he combines his personal story of becoming a writer with a practical account of how he works. In the autobiographical sections, he reveals his early encounters with storytelling, his struggles before getting published for the first time and how writing fits into the rest of his life. He also explores the practical aspects of writing, including vocabulary, grammar, description, dialogue and revision. His approach is direct and conversational. The book also features a marked-up manuscript that indicates actual revisions, which can be helpful for writers thinking about the process of editing. Overall, King offers encouragement and technical advice for first-time novelists.

Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life.

Recent findings suggest that anne Lamott starts this book with a family story. Her brother left a report about birds until the last minute and felt overwhelmed by everything he had to do. Their father told him to take it bird by bird, inspiring the title of the book. That small instruction becomes the book’s central approach to writing. Instead of confronting the project as an impossible whole, attend to one manageable piece at a time. Lamott applies that approach to rough drafts and the emotional confusion of creative work. She offers humor and permission to produce messy drafts. Her advice is to reduce the task into bite-sized parts, accept imperfection and continue even when there is no guarantee of a future reward.

Writing Down the Bones: Freeing the Writer Within.

Sources indicate that in this book, popular author Natalie Goldberg approaches writing as a practice strengthened through repetition. She offers short reflections and exercises that help writers get words onto the page before their inner judgment shuts them down. The exercises provide a low-pressure space for discovering memories, images and even unexpected connections. The focus is on developing an open relationship with the act of writing. Goldberg pushes writers to keep the hand moving and resist the urge to cross out thoughts immediately. These small habits help the writer notice more and censor less when creating material. If you spend more time evaluating possible sentences rather than writing them, this is the book for you. It has sold more than one million copies.

Story Genius: How to Use Brain Science to Go Beyond Outlining and Write a Riveting Novel (Before You Waste Three Years Writing 327 Pages That Go Nowhere).

Author Lisa Cron is a story coach, speaker and author who has previously worked as a literary agent. She asks writers to look beneath the surface events of a story. In other words, an unusual situation or dramatic accident is not enough by itself. What matters is how that event affects a particular person, given that person’s unique worldview. Her method places the protagonist’s internal struggle at the center of the novel’s development. The book moves from an initial idea to a developed blueprint, including scenes. Its aim is to connect incidents through a protagonist’s changing interiority. Read this when you know what happens in your novel but cannot explain why it matters to the main character living through it.

Save the Cat! Writes a Novel: The Last Book On Novel Writing You’ll Ever Need.

Recent findings suggest that jessica Brody is the bestselling author of more than 20 novels, mainly young adult fiction. This book organizes story structure around 15 major developments, extending from the opening image to the finale. It also introduces 10 story categories based on patterns of conflict and transformation, giving writers ways to understand the kind of narrative they are building. The appeal is clarity. The writer can examine the purpose of different turning points in their novel. What releases the central journey? When does the situation change? How does the ending express what the protagonist has learned? Read this if your first novel feels exciting in fragments but isn’t coming together as a whole.

Plot & Structure (Write Great Fiction).

Former trial lawyer James Scott Bell offers a practical guide to creating a plot and understanding how its parts fit together. He addresses the relationship between plot and structure and the differences between commercial and literary fiction. The emphasis is on usable techniques. Bell’s central framework is called LOCK, which stands for lead, objective, confrontation and knockout. These elements direct attention toward a compelling central character, a clear goal, meaningful opposition and a strong ending. Using these attributes, you can decide if a story has enough pressure and direction to sustain the reader’s interest. What is your protagonist trying to achieve? What prevents success? What would make the resolution satisfying?

Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story.

Author Ursula K. Le Guin turns her attention to the language by which a story reaches the reader. Her writing guide combines discussion with exercises. She walks readers through drills in storytelling, point of view and grammar. The exercises make this a book to use actively. Le Guin says that the work of a sentence is to carry the reader to the next one. She addresses how to handle exposition, or how to incorporate information into a story instead of allowing explanation to bring it to a halt. Her approach connects elements sometimes treated separately, like language and pacing. The value of this book is helping readers hear and inspect their prose. A promising plot still needs solid sentences that keep the story moving.

This style manual was privately printed in 1918 for Cornell University students by English professor William Strunk Jr., then published more widely by Harcourt in 1920. Strunk’s former student and author E. B. White revised and expanded the volume in 1959. This book concentrates on constructing clear prose. It is short, about 100 pages, which means it is perfect to consult regularly as you write. Its usefulness lies in directing a writer’s attention toward language. A novelist might be absorbed in a character’s choices while giving too little thought to how to clearly communicate those behaviors in a sentence. Strunk and White set the stage for authors to learn the conventions of clear prose. They provide a foundation from which to make deliberate stylistic choices that enhance a reader’s experience.

The Writing Life: The Classic Essay Collection on the Creative Process.

Annie Dillard, a Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist with experience writing fiction and nonfiction, published poetry, essays, prose and literary criticism. In The Writing Life, she offers a reflection on creative writing, not a step-by-step manual. She considers the difficulty and uncertainty of the writing process. A line of words can lead a writer into unfamiliar territory, but they may not know where to go next. What first appears promising might actually be a dead end, while a seemingly incidental encounter might become the real subject. Dillard preserves a place for the parts of writing that remain difficult, even when the writer is attentive and experienced. She offers perspective on the patience and seriousness of writing.

Refuse to Be Done: How to Write and Rewrite a Novel in Three Drafts.

Writer and teacher Matt Bell treats revision as a central part of novel writing. His guide divides the process into three broad stages, giving each step a different purpose. The first move helps writers generate material and move through the initial draft. The second focuses on reworking the narrative through outlining, modeling and rewriting. The third step turns toward a layered polishing process. This final stage breaks revision into specific operations, deconstructing a large and potentially overwhelming task into a series of more manageable actions. This book is worth reading before writing the first page. It offers a practical guide to making a manuscript stronger.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The firm started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond manufacturer agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

Sources indicate that the five-year-old tech giant was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he mentioned.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the manufacturer.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a new entrepreneurial boom.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve seen this before: Upcoming technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a new entrepreneurial boom.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve seen this before: Upcoming technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

Sources indicate that business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for new registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

What’s driving that growth? It’s not a single engine but a combination of forces, including the continued popularity of remote work and the appeal of being your own boss and having more financial freedom, both now more within reach because of AI.

If you previously dropped a business idea because it seemed too complicated or expensive, now may be the time to reconsider. AI has reached a level of capability that didn’t exist just a few years ago. It’s steadily eroding traditional startup barriers, helping founders turn even ambitious ideas into real businesses with less money, fewer employees and fewer outside resources.

It has been revealed that until recently, launching a manufacturer often meant spending money before making money. Office space, equipment, expensive software and employees with specialized skills were requirements in most sectors, not to mention the accountants and consultants needed just to get started.

In a recent development, now, cloud infrastructure has replaced costly servers. No-code platforms make it possible to build websites and apps without extensive programming knowledge. E-commerce platforms give small companies access to national and global markets. Generative AI accelerates this trend by helping entrepreneurs research markets, analyze competitors, draft business plans, develop marketing campaigns, create content and automate tedious administrative work.

It has been revealed that start by asking yourself, “What do I need to reach customers at this stage, and how will it maximize my return on investment?” Use inexpensive tools to create a product prototype, a landing page or a basic marketing campaign. Talk to potential customers. Test your pricing and measure the response. Save major investments for ideas that show real demand.

AI gives founders a chance to rethink hiring. Entrepreneurs once had to hire employees or contractors before they were generating enough revenue to support them. Today, a solo founder with the right AI tools can handle many of those functions alone.

In a recent development, that doesn’t mean putting complete trust in a chatbot. AI-assisted work still requires human oversight, judgment, verification and refinement. And when you’re building a trustworthy brand from scratch, you have to consider accuracy, privacy and legal challenges.

Use AI to draft routine marketing emails, but hire an experienced marketer when strategy matters. Organize basic finances with bookkeeping software, but consult an accountant for key tax decisions. Automate answers to repetitive customer service questions, but keep a human in the loop for complicated interactions or when customers ask for one. The goal isn’t to eliminate employees. It’s to delay fixed expenses until your business can support them.

According to recent reports, historically, founders moved to places like San Francisco or Austin because those cities offered concentrated pools of money and talent. Those hubs remain vibrant, but AI and remote technology are reducing the importance of location.

Recent findings suggest that A tech founder in a small town can use the same AI platforms and cloud services as someone in Silicon Valley. Remote collaboration provides access to talent anywhere, and e-commerce can reach customers far beyond a manufacturer’s hometown.

With AI tools, you can explore many ideas from almost anywhere. Instead of asking, “Where does my business need to be based?” you can ask, “Where would I like to live while I grow my business?” That kind of freedom can make a real difference in your quality of life.

Recent findings suggest that forming a business and building a successful one are different things. Many of the companies registered this year will never become fully operational. Others will struggle to find customers or stay profitable. AI can’t fix a weak business model, create demand where none exists or eliminate the financial risks of entrepreneurship.

In a recent development, what AI can do is make the process easier and cheaper, and therein lies the lesson. Instead of investing heavily up front in one untested concept, make a series of small bets. Develop a minimum viable product. Test marketing messages. Experiment with prices. Ask AI to identify the assumptions in your business plan, then test them with real customers and real-world data.

According to recent reports, with more than 5 million businesses formed since the start of 2026, the U.S. could finish the year with close to 7 million fresh registrations if the current pace continues. There’s evidence that AI may be contributing to that momentum. But like the steam engine, electricity, the internet and smartphones before it, AI is a tool. The real power lies with entrepreneurs who are willing to start lean, test early, automate selectively and spend strategically. With that approach, we may see a boom not only in startups with potential but, more importantly, in businesses that endure.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a fresh entrepreneurial boom.

In a recent development, we’ve seen this before: New technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

Business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for fresh registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the manufacturer announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock owners into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

It has been revealed that true, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including massive-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

#87587. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1736 w)

How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token.
  • Recent findings suggest that using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine.
  • They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Recent findings suggest that using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Industry observers note that setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

According to recent reports, gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Recent findings suggest that every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

It has been revealed that the limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

Recent findings suggest that the docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is unveiled, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

Sources indicate that the docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

It has been revealed that that makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

Sources indicate that italy’s largest banking group, Intesa Sanpaolo, increased its spot altcoin ETF holdings according to a newly introduced disclosure. This follows capital rotation out of Bitcoin products by a slew of traditional firms amid dwindling market sentiment.

In a recent development, the bank’s disclosed crypto ETF holdings grew in Q3 2026 to $108.56 million, up $17 million, while digital asset prices moved sideways. In June, total assets were worth $90 million as it looked to diversify and grow holdings systematically.

According to recent reports, bitcoin, the largest asset in the portfolio, was reduced to make room for altcoins in a possible bid to diversify assets. At the end of Q2, BTC holdings stood at $69.32 million but dropped slightly to above $61 million last quarter. The firm’s Ethereum exposure also dropped to $5 million.

However, Solana and XRP products filled the vacuum, highlighting institutional appetite for these assets. At the time of writing, the bank’s spot Solana ETF exposure is at $14.1 million after its investment in the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF ballooned from seven shares to 875,407 shares.

Industry observers note that intesa’s XRP investment also grew over the same period to $27.2 million, driven mainly by 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF. The firm’s shares in the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF remained unchanged across both quarters.

More broadly, the bank reduced its Bitcoin ETF exposure and increased SOL and XRP products. Most experts believe it follows the current market trend, and firms, especially traditional companies, need to diversify to make up for Bitcoin’s decline.

Historically, during bear phases, there’s a huge rotation of capital into altcoins, though it’s not sustained for long. As expected, Solana and XRP become institutional favorites, while Ethereum trades similarly to Bitcoin.

Recent findings suggest that the former have the potential to record spikes within the red wave, like in 2022 before the approval of spot ETF products in the United States. These products opened up digital assets to a new stash of traditional capital.

It has been revealed that intesa and other banks have since increased their crypto exposure, driven by the need to diversify assets and a broader adoption spree. Heightened institutional and retail interests pushed Bitcoin to an all-time high above $125k last year. Currently, BTC trades at $63,819, while Ethereum is slightly below $1,800.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (365 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and issue unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.
  • According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and problem Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.
  • Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and issue unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.

According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and problem Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.

Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.

Combined, the total value of the affected assets stood at around $1.06 million, per Onchain Lens.

Following the hack, the funds were transferred through the decentralized exchange Uniswap and multiple crypto wallets, making it challenging to trace their final destination.

It has been revealed that the attack targeted Gonka AI's cross-chain bridge. The cross-chain bridge makes it possible to transfer assets from Gonka AI's native chain to Ethereum and vice versa.

According to the project's technical documentation, withdrawing funds from Gonka to Ethereum requires certain cryptographic signatures from the network's validator set.

The cryptographic signatures are checked against the BLS group key, which changes with every network epoch.

Per the report, the attacker was able to change the epoch BLS group key on the bridge, making it possible for the hacker to control the part of the bridge responsible for authorizing fund withdrawals.

Thus, the hacker was able to withdraw funds from the bridge's stablecoin reserves and issue WGNK tokens without locking the required amount of assets on the native blockchain.

Blockchain security firm Blockaid noted that the hack had taken place, with the total amount of funds stolen reaching about $1.05 million across roughly five transactions at the time of the initial alert.

At the time it spotted the suspicious activity, Blockaid noted that the hack was still ongoing.

Onchain Lens's numbers differ slightly, with the firm reporting around $884,800 in stablecoin withdrawals and $172,000 in unbacked WGNK issuance.

Notably, the issuance of unbacked tokens presents an additional problem, given that such tokens could potentially enter circulation without the necessary reserves to back them.

Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

Sources indicate that to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Industry observers note that much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

It has been revealed that by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old organization raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

Sources indicate that san Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor indicates it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a Latest York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

In a recent development, agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, unveiled a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of substantial rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid promptly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he mentioned.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

In a recent development, nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he remarked. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk manufacturer developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

Sources indicate that “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd noted. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

It has been revealed that in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who stated the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he stated, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

According to recent reports, in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion organization Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

In a recent development, A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

Recent findings suggest that while the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd remarked he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd stated there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

Sources indicate that the firm now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

#87581. This Is the Reason Your AI Tools Actually Remember Anything
